current: God is furious at the lack of faith and decrees that the entire generation will die in the desert over forty years — only their children will enter the land.
problem: The decree covers those counted in the census from age twenty up who complained, not the entire generation; Caleb and Joshua are also exempted, so 'only their children' is not exact.
evidence: Numbers 14:29-30: 'Of all of you who were recorded in your various lists from the age of twenty years up, you who have muttered against Me, none shall enter the land ... save Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun.' https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.14.29-30
fix: God decrees that everyone counted from age twenty and up who complained will die in the desert over forty years; only their children, with Caleb and Joshua, will enter the land.

current: They return carrying enormous grape clusters on a pole as proof of the land's fertility, and ten of the twelve deliver a report laced with demoralization: the cities are fortified and enormous, the people are like giants ('we seemed like grasshoppers in our own eyes, and so we seemed in their eyes'), and conquest is impossible.
problem: The verse describes a single cluster of grapes carried on a pole by two men, plus pomegranates and figs, not several clusters. 'Enormous' and 'as proof of fertility' go slightly beyond the verse, though 13:27 has them show the fruit.
evidence: Numbers 13:23: 'they cut down a branch with a single cluster of grapes—it had to be borne on a carrying frame by two of them—and some pomegranates and figs' (Heb. ואשכול ענבים אחד וישאהו במוט בשנים). https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.13.23
fix: They return carrying a single cluster of grapes on a pole between two men, with pomegranates and figs, and ten of the twelve deliver a report laced with demoralization: the cities are fortified and enormous, the people are like giants ('we seemed like grasshoppers in our own eyes, and so we seemed in their eyes'), and conquest is impossible.

current: The phrase 'we seemed like grasshoppers in our own eyes — and so we seemed in their eyes' is the Torah's most devastating piece of psychological insight: the spies have no way of knowing how the Canaanites perceive them, yet they project their own self-image onto their enemies. The rabbis note that this inner defeat preceded any military failure.
problem: States one modern reading as fact and attributes it vaguely to 'the rabbis' with no source. The Talmud raises the question and gives two answers: Rav Mesharshiya calls the spies liars on this point, and the Gemara answers that they overheard the Canaanites call them grasshoppers. 'Most devastating' is an editorial superlative.
evidence: Sotah 35a: 'Rav Mesharshiyya says: The spies were liars ... "And so were we in their eyes," from where could they have known this? The Gemara responds: ... From there they heard the Canaanites saying: We see people who look like grasshoppers in the trees.' https://www.sefaria.org/Sotah.35a
fix: The spies say 'we looked like grasshoppers to ourselves, and so we must have looked to them' (Numbers 13:33). The Talmud (Sotah 35a) asks how they could know what the Canaanites thought: one rabbi says they were lying, and another answer says they overheard the Canaanites calling them grasshoppers.

current: The day the spies returned with their bad report — the ninth of Av (Tisha B'Av) — became the most catastrophic date in Jewish history: the first Temple was destroyed on that date, the second Temple was destroyed on that date, and numerous other disasters are associated with it in tradition.
problem: The date of the spies' report and of the First Temple's destruction on 9 Av are rabbinic tradition, stated here as plain fact. The Bible itself dates the First Temple's burning to the 7th (2 Kings 25:8) and the 10th of Av (Jeremiah 52:12); the Talmud reconciles these. 'Most catastrophic date in Jewish history' is an unsourced superlative.
evidence: Mishnah Taanit 4:6: 'On the Ninth of Av it was decreed upon our ancestors that they would all die in the wilderness ... and the Temple was destroyed the first time ... and the second time' https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Taanit.4.6 ; Taanit 29a: 'That night was the night of the Ninth of Av' and cites 2 Kings 25:8 ('on the seventh day') and Jeremiah 52:12 ('on the tenth day'), concluding the Temple was set on fire on the ninth. https://www.sefaria.org/Taanit.29a
fix: According to the Talmud (Taanit 29a), the night the people wept over the spies' report was the ninth of Av (Tisha B'Av), and the Mishnah (Taanit 4:6) lists other disasters on that date, including the destruction of the First and Second Temples.

current: The Talmud (Sotah 35a) derives from this story the principle that lashon hara (evil speech) about the land of Israel is as serious as evil speech about people.
problem: Wrong source and reversed argument. The teaching is in Arakhin 15a, not Sotah 35a, and it argues from lesser to greater: if speaking badly about the land was punished so severely, speaking badly about a person is worse.
evidence: Arakhin 15a: 'Rabbi Elazar ben Perata says: Come and see how great the power of malicious speech is ... if one who defames the wood and rocks of Eretz Yisrael received such a severe punishment, then with regard to one who defames another person, all the more so will he be punished severely.' https://www.sefaria.org/Arakhin.15a
fix: The Talmud (Arakhin 15a) reasons from this story that if the spies were punished so severely for speaking badly about the wood and stones of the land of Israel, someone who speaks badly about another person will be punished even more.

current: Tisha B'Av, the fast day commemorating both Temple destructions, is rooted in this night when Israel wept without cause and was told by God: 'I will give you cause to weep in all future generations.'
problem: The link to Tisha B'Av and God's words are a Talmudic teaching, but here they are stated as the Torah's own narrative; the Torah does not contain this statement.
evidence: Sotah 35a: 'Rabba says that Rabbi Yoḥanan says: That day was the eve of the Ninth of Av, and the Holy One, Blessed be He, said: On that day they wept a gratuitous weeping, so I will establish that day for them as a day of weeping for the future generations.' https://www.sefaria.org/Sotah.35a (also Taanit 29a)
fix: The Talmud (Sotah 35a; Taanit 29a) links Tisha B'Av, the fast day commemorating both Temple destructions, to this night, teaching that because Israel wept without cause, God set the day as a day of weeping for future generations.

current: The Late Bronze Age Canaan the spies were sent to scout was genuinely fortified and urbanized. Cities like Hazor (the largest city in Canaan at its peak) had massive rampart walls and palace complexes; Megiddo, Lachish, and Gezer were similarly imposing. Egyptian Execration Texts and the Amarna Letters confirm the political complexity and military strength of Canaanite city-states. The 'giants' (Nephilim) mentioned by the spies may reflect the Israelites' encounter with chariot-owning professional armies — a technology they had never faced — translated into the language of superhuman beings.
problem: Places the spies in the Late Bronze Age as settled fact, and gets the archaeology backwards: most Late Bronze Age Canaanite towns had no city wall (only Hazor, Megiddo and possibly Gezer among the big cities). The Execration Texts are mostly earlier (Middle Kingdom), and the Amarna Letters show Canaanite rulers begging Egypt for troops, not military strength. The Nephilim-as-chariot-armies idea is unsourced speculation.
evidence: Mazar via biblicalhistoricalcontext.com: 'from the time of Thutmose III until the end of Egyptian rule, almost all towns in Canaan had no city wall ... Excluding Hazor, Megiddo, and (possibly) Gezer ... the only towns with walls constructed in the Late Bronze age are Ashdod, Tel Abu Hawam, and Tel Beit Misrim' https://biblicalhistoricalcontext.com/israelite-origins/israelite-origins-egyptian-domination-of-canaan/ ; Wikipedia Tel Hazor: 'From the Middle Bronze Age (around 1750 BCE) to the Iron Age (ninth century BCE), Hazor was the largest fortified city in the region' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tel_Hazor ; Wikipedia Amarna letters: Abdi-Heba 'repeatedly pleads with the pharaoh ... for military assistance' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amarna_letters
fix: The Torah does not tie the spies' mission to an archaeological period. In the Late Bronze Age, when Egypt ruled Canaan, Hazor was the largest fortified city in the region, and Megiddo and probably Gezer were walled, but most Canaanite towns had no city wall. The Amarna Letters, written by Canaanite rulers to Egypt in the 1300s BCE, show many small city-states that pleaded with Egypt for troops.

current: The next day the community blames Moses and a plague begins, killed only when Aaron runs into the crowd with incense to atone.
problem: Word error: the plague was 'stopped', not 'killed'. Also the community blamed Moses and Aaron together.
evidence: Numbers 17:6: 'the whole Israelite community railed against Moses and Aaron, saying, "You two have brought death upon GOD's people!"'; 17:13 'he stood between the dead and the living until the plague was checked.' https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.17.6-13
fix: The next day the community blames Moses and Aaron and a plague begins, stopped only when Aaron runs into the crowd with incense to atone.

current: The confrontation at the Tabernacle entrance ends with God telling Moses and Aaron to separate from the congregation so divine fury can consume them; Moses successfully intercedes again; but then the earth opens below Korach, Datan, Abiram, and their households — they go down alive into the pit with all their possessions — and fire from God consumes the 250 men offering incense.
problem: Both Moses and Aaron fall on their faces and plead, not Moses alone. Also 'their households' should not suggest all of Korach's family died: the Torah later says Korach's sons did not die.
evidence: Numbers 16:22: 'But they fell on their faces and said, "O God ... When one member sins, will You be wrathful with the whole community?"' https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.16.22 ; Numbers 26:11: 'The sons of Korah, however, did not die.' https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.26.11
fix: The confrontation at the Tabernacle entrance ends with God telling Moses and Aaron to separate from the congregation so divine fury can consume them; Moses and Aaron successfully plead again; but then the earth opens below Korach, Datan, Abiram, and their households (though Korach's sons did not die, Numbers 26:11) — they go down alive into the pit with all their possessions — and fire from God consumes the 250 men offering incense.

current: Korach's argument — 'the entire community is holy, every one of them' — is a direct quote from Leviticus 19:2 ('you shall be holy'), making it a case where scripture is used to argue against the very authority that transmitted scripture.
problem: Not a quote. Numbers 16:3 says 'all the community are holy, all of them' (כל העדה כלם קדשים); Leviticus 19:2 says 'You shall be holy' (קדשים תהיו). They share only the word 'holy'.
evidence: Numbers 16:3 Heb. 'כִּי כׇל־הָעֵדָה כֻּלָּם קְדֹשִׁים' https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.16.3 ; Leviticus 19:2 Heb. 'קְדֹשִׁים תִּהְיוּ כִּי קָדוֹשׁ אֲנִי' https://www.sefaria.org/Leviticus.19.2
fix: Korach's argument, 'all the community are holy, all of them' (Numbers 16:3), uses the same word for 'holy' as God's command in Leviticus 19:2, 'You shall be holy.'

current: In the Talmud (Avot 5:17), Korach's name became shorthand for illegitimate power grabs dressed up in the language of justice.
problem: Avot is a tractate of the Mishnah, not the Talmud, and Avot 5:17 does not say this; it names 'Korah and all his congregation' as the example of a dispute not for the sake of Heaven, which the previous sentence already says.
evidence: Pirkei Avot 5:17: 'And which is the controversy that is not for the sake of Heaven? Such was the controversy of Korah and all his congregation.' https://www.sefaria.org/Pirkei_Avot.5.17
fix: Cut the sentence. (The preceding sentence already covers Avot 5:17; if a citation is wanted there, add '(Mishnah Avot 5:17)' after 'for the sake of heaven.'')

current: The rebellion of Korach has been interpreted throughout Jewish history as the paradigmatic warning against populist challenges to legitimate religious authority — and equally as a caution against abuse of authority that invites such challenges. Medieval biblical commentators noted that Korach's argument about universal holiness was not wrong in principle but was wrong in timing and motivation: the ideal of a 'kingdom of priests and a holy nation' (Exodus 19:6) is the goal, but the path to it requires gradual sanctification, not the abolition of all distinctions.
problem: No commentator is named and no source was found for the 'wrong in timing' / 'gradual sanctification' reading, or for the claim that the story has been read 'equally' as a warning against abuse of authority. The sourced traditional reading is that Korach was motivated by a grievance over the priesthood (Rashi on 16:1) and that his was a dispute not for the sake of Heaven (Avot 5:17).
evidence: Rashi on Numbers 16:1: 'He betook himself on one side ... so that he might raise a protest regarding the priesthood to which Moses had appointed his brother.' https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Numbers.16.1 ; Pirkei Avot 5:17 https://www.sefaria.org/Pirkei_Avot.5.17
fix: Jewish tradition reads the rebellion of Korach as a warning against challenges to legitimate authority driven by personal ambition: Rashi on 16:1 says Korach was protesting the priesthood Moses had given to his brother Aaron.

current: The phrase 'standing between the living and the dead' — Aaron with his incense stopping the plague — became a paradigm for priestly intercession and is referenced in later Jewish martyrology.
problem: The verse is right (17:13), but no source was found for its being 'referenced in later Jewish martyrology' or made a 'paradigm'.
evidence: Numbers 17:13: 'he stood between the dead and the living until the plague was checked.' https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.17.13 ; no source found for the martyrology claim.
fix: The image of Aaron with his incense, standing 'between the dead and the living until the plague was checked' (Numbers 17:13), shows a priest's atonement protecting the people.

current: The rebellion of Korach, Datan, and Abiram draws on a political reality attested throughout the ancient Near East: the tension between hereditary priestly elites and broader social groups who resented monopolized access to the divine.
problem: A sweeping historical claim with no source, presented as settled; nothing fetched supports it.
evidence: No source found. Numbers 16:2 (quoted in the next sentence of this field) is the only sourced part of the field. https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.16.2
fix: Cut the sentence.

current: The narrative's resolution — miraculous earth-swallowing, fire from heaven, and a blooming staff — uses spectacular divine intervention to settle what was fundamentally a political conflict over religious authority.
problem: Presents a secular-critical reading ('fundamentally a political conflict') as fact. The Torah presents the dispute as a challenge to God's choice (16:5, 17:20).
evidence: Numbers 17:20: 'The staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout, and I will rid Myself of the incessant mutterings of the Israelites against you.' https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.17.20 ; 16:32-35 https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.16.32-35
fix: The Torah settles the dispute through divine signs: the earth swallowing the rebels, fire from God consuming the 250 men, and Aaron's staff sprouting to show whom God had chosen.

current: The people erupt at Moses and Aaron ('why did you bring us out of Egypt to die?'), and God tells Moses to speak to a rock to bring water — but Moses, at the end of his endurance, strikes it twice instead and berates the people: 'Shall we bring you water from this rock?'
problem: The quoted line is a blend of two verses, not a quote. In 20:4-5 the people ask why they were brought into the wilderness to die and why they were taken out of Egypt to this wretched place. Moses also speaks ('Listen, you rebels...') before striking, not after.
evidence: Numbers 20:4-5: 'Why have you brought GOD's congregation into this wilderness for us and our livestock to die there? Why did you make us leave Egypt to bring us to this wretched place...' ; 20:10-11: '"Listen, you rebels, shall we get water for you out of this rock?" And Moses raised his hand and struck the rock twice with his rod.' https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.20.4-11
fix: The people erupt at Moses and Aaron ('Why did you make us leave Egypt to bring us to this wretched place?'), and God tells Moses to speak to a rock to bring water, but Moses berates the people, 'Listen, you rebels, shall we get water for you out of this rock?', and strikes the rock twice.

current: The rabbis offered dozens of explanations: he spoke angrily to the people, he gave himself and Aaron credit ('shall WE bring you water?'), he struck the rock twice suggesting doubt.
problem: 'Dozens' is unsupported: Or HaChaim counts ten approaches. The view about the second strike says the fault was striking a second time, not that it 'suggested doubt'. The 'credit' view is Rabbeinu Chananel and Ramban.
evidence: Or HaChaim on Numbers 20:8: 'I have come across 10 different approaches ... 3) G'd's anger was caused by Moses hitting the rock a second time ... 7) Rabbeynu Chananel and Nachmanides after him claim that what angered G'd was that Moses portrayed himself and Aaron as producing the water by saying נוציא לכם מים.' https://www.sefaria.org/Or_HaChaim_on_Numbers.20.8
fix: Commentators offered many explanations (the Or HaChaim lists ten): he spoke angrily to the people, he spoke as if he and Aaron were producing the water ('shall we get water for you?'), or he struck the rock a second time.

current: The bronze serpent Moses made (Nechushtan) was kept by Israel and eventually became an object of illicit worship, requiring King Hezekiah to destroy it six centuries later (2 Kings 18:4).
problem: 'Six centuries later' assumes a date for the Exodus and matches neither the traditional count nor a stated source; the Bible gives no such interval. The name Nehushtan appears only in 2 Kings 18:4, in Hezekiah's time.
evidence: 2 Kings 18:4: 'He also broke into pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made, for until that time the Israelites had been offering sacrifices to it; it was called Nehushtan.' https://www.sefaria.org/II_Kings.18.4
fix: The bronze serpent Moses made survived for centuries: 2 Kings 18:4 says King Hezekiah broke it into pieces because the Israelites had been offering sacrifices to it, and that it was called Nehushtan.

current: The Talmud (Yoma 67b) states that the nations will mock Israel for this commandment, and God's response is essentially: obey it anyway.
problem: Yoma 67b's list of statutes that 'Satan and the nations of the world challenge' is pork, shaatnez, chalitza, the leper's purification and the scapegoat; it does not include the red heifer. The red heifer version is in Rashi on Numbers 19:2 (from Midrash Tanchuma).
evidence: Yoma 67b: 'matters that Satan and the nations of the world challenge ... They are: The prohibitions against eating pork; wearing ... wool and linen; performing the ḥalitza ceremony ...; the purification ceremony of the leper; and the scapegoat.' https://www.sefaria.org/Yoma.67b ; Rashi on Numbers 19:2: 'Because Satan and the nations of the world taunt Israel, saying, "What is this command ..." ... It is an enactment from before Me; you have no right to criticize it.' https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Numbers.19.2
fix: Rashi on Numbers 19:2 says that Satan and the nations taunt Israel over this commandment, and that the Torah calls it a chok to say: it is a decree from God, and you have no right to question it.

current: Both kingdoms are located in modern Jordan; Og of Bashan became legendary for his size ('his iron bed was nine cubits long' — Deuteronomy 3:11).
problem: Bashan lies in modern Syria and Jordan, and its western part is the Golan Heights; it is not only in Jordan.
evidence: Wikipedia, Bashan: 'It is situated in modern-day Jordan and Syria. Its western part, nowadays known as the Golan Heights, was occupied by Israel during the 1967 Six Day War.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bashan ; Deuteronomy 3:11 'an iron bedstead ... nine cubits long' https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.3.11
fix: Sihon's kingdom lay in what is now Jordan, and Bashan spanned parts of modern Syria and Jordan, including the Golan Heights; Og of Bashan became legendary for his size ('his iron bed was nine cubits long' — Deuteronomy 3:11).

current: The route of march through Edom, Moab, and Ammon tracks through the Transjordanian plateau, a real geographical corridor known from Egyptian records and archaeology.
problem: The Torah says Israel did not march through Edom: Edom refused passage on the King's Highway and Israel went around it. Israel also stopped at the border of Ammon. The 'known from Egyptian records' claim is unsourced.
evidence: Numbers 20:21: 'So Edom would not let Israel cross their territory, and Israel turned away from them.' ; 21:4: 'to skirt the land of Edom' ; 21:24: 'from the Arnon to the Jabbok, as far as [Az] of the Ammonites' https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.20.21 ; https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.21.4 ; https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.21.24 ; Deuteronomy 2:19 'do not harass them' (Ammon) https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.2.19
fix: Edom refused to let Israel use the King's Highway through its land, so Israel went around Edom (Numbers 20:17-21; 21:4), and its conquest of Sihon's land stopped at the border of Ammon (Numbers 21:24).
